questions.stem: What does electronegativity measure?

options.text: An atom's power to attract the shared pair in a covalent bond toward itself
options.explanation: The definition centres on the bonded pair.

options.text: An atom's ability to lose its own electrons
options.explanation: That describes ionisation tendency, not electronegativity.

options.text: The total charge of an ion
options.explanation: Electronegativity applies to bonded atoms, not formal ionic charge.

options.text: The mass-to-charge ratio of an atom
options.explanation: Mass plays no role in the definition.

questions.stem: What happens to electron distribution when bonded atoms differ in electronegativity?

options.explanation: Shared electrons remain in motion.

options.text: It becomes unsymmetrical, denser around the more electronegative atom
options.explanation: The stronger pull shifts the shared density.
Evenness belongs to equal electronegativities.

options.text: The electrons transfer completely to one atom
options.explanation: Complete transfer is ionic bonding; here sharing persists, unevenly.

questions.stem: Which scale assigns electronegativity values to atoms?

options.explanation: pH measures acidity.
Atomic number counts protons, not pulling power.
It is the numbering system of record here.
Kelvin measures temperature.

questions.stem: Which element tops the electronegativity table, and at what Pauling value?

options.explanation: Oxygen is high but not the record holder.
Chlorine trails fluorine.
Caesium sits at the low end.
The strongest puller sits at the top of the scale.

questions.stem: Why does a nucleus attract the shared pair toward itself in a bond?

options.text: Its positive charge draws the negatively charged outer-shell electrons
options.explanation: Opposite charges attract; density shifts toward the stronger nucleus.
Neutrons carry no charge.

options.text: Its electrons push the pair across
options.explanation: Electron-electron repulsion cannot confer a pull toward one side.
Mass is not the operative force.

questions.stem: Define electronegativity.
questions.modelAnswer: Electronegativity rates the power of a bonded atom to pull the shared pair of a covalent bond toward itself.

questions.stem: Name the scale used for electronegativity values and the element at its top.
questions.modelAnswer: The Pauling scale assigns the values, and fluorine tops it at 4.0.

questions.stem: Explain why differing electronegativities produce an unsymmetrical electron distribution.
questions.modelAnswer: Both nuclei attract the same bonding pair, but with unequal strength; the stronger, more electronegative nucleus wins a larger share of the electron density, so the distribution loses symmetry.

questions.stem: In the C-F bond of fluoromethane, state which end holds the electron density more tightly and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine holds the density: as the most electronegative element (4.0) it pulls the bonding pair harder than carbon, so electron density concentrates at the fluorine end.

questions.stem: Which electronegativity relationship favours ionic bond formation?

options.explanation: Zero difference is the nonpolar limit.

options.text: A large difference between the two atoms
options.explanation: Big mismatch tears the pair into ions.

options.text: A small difference between the two atoms
options.explanation: Matched pulls share covalently.
That gives a purely nonpolar covalent bond.

questions.stem: A bond has an electronegativity difference of 1.2 on the Pauling scale. What type is it?

options.explanation: Nonpolar requires near-zero difference.
Metallic bonding is a different class entirely.

options.text: Polar covalent, within the 0.3 to 1.7 band
options.explanation: Unequal but incomplete sharing.
Ionic territory begins above 1.7.

questions.stem: In a polar bond, which atom carries the delta-negative charge?

options.explanation: It ends up delta-positive.
The poles exist precisely because the sharing is unequal.
Electronegativity, not mass, assigns the poles.
It draws the shared electrons closer.

questions.stem: What is true of the charge centres in a polar bond?

options.text: The negative and positive charge centres do not coincide
options.explanation: Asymmetric density splits the centres.
Coincidence belongs to nonpolar bonds.
One centre stays positive.
The separated centres are the definition.

questions.stem: As the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms grows, the bond

options.text: loses its covalent character instantly at any difference
options.explanation: Small differences leave the bond covalent.

options.text: becomes more polar, approaching ionic character
options.explanation: The sharing grows ever more one-sided.
The difference drives polarity upward.
Polarity tracks the difference.

questions.stem: State the Pauling-scale rule of thumb that separates ionic from covalent bond formation.
questions.modelAnswer: An electronegativity difference of 2 or more leads to ionic bonding; less than 2 leads to covalent bonding.

questions.stem: State the electronegativity-difference band that produces polar covalent bonds.
questions.modelAnswer: Differences from 0.3 to 1.7 produce polar covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Explain why a large electronegativity difference ends in electron transfer rather than sharing.
questions.modelAnswer: When one nucleus out-pulls the other by a wide margin, the shared pair is drawn so close to the stronger atom that it effectively belongs to it - the sharing regime collapses into full transfer and ions form.

questions.stem: Bond X has a Pauling difference of 2.5; bond Y has 0.9. Classify both and name the delta end of Y's more electronegative atom.
questions.modelAnswer: X is ionic - its difference exceeds 2; Y is polar covalent, sitting in the 0.3-1.7 band, with delta-negative on its more electronegative atom.

questions.stem: What does the dipole moment measure?

options.explanation: Strength is not the dipole's reading.

options.text: How many bonds a molecule has
options.explanation: Counting bonds is simple arithmetic, not a dipole property.
It quantifies the bond's charge separation.
Bond length is a separate quantity.

questions.stem: Which way does the dipole arrow point?

options.explanation: The arrow runs the other way.

options.text: Toward the larger atom by size
options.explanation: The pole assignment follows polarity, not size.
The convention is fixed.

options.text: Toward the partially negative end of the dipole
options.explanation: The crossed arrow points delta-negative.

questions.stem: Which two considerations decide whether a polyatomic molecule is polar?

options.text: The polarity of each bond and how the bonds are arranged
options.explanation: Both vector size and geometry matter.

options.text: The polarity of each bond only
options.explanation: Arrangement can cancel the sum.
Mass never decides polarity.
Counting atoms misses both polarity and geometry.

questions.stem: Why is CCl4 nonpolar despite four polar C-Cl bonds?

options.text: The molecule carries a net charge
options.explanation: CCl4 is neutral and nonpolar.

options.text: Its individual dipole moments cancel each other out by symmetry
options.explanation: Four equal arrows pointing outward in tetrahedral geometry sum to zero.
Each C-Cl bond is polar; the molecule is not.
Chlorine is strongly electronegative.

questions.stem: Why is CH3Cl polar?

options.explanation: Cancellation would make it nonpolar.
CH3Cl is a neutral molecule.

options.text: Its polar bonds do not cancel - the net dipole points toward the chlorine
options.explanation: The single chlorine breaks the symmetry of the four bonds.
The C-Cl bond is polar.

questions.stem: Define the dipole moment and its arrow convention.
questions.modelAnswer: The dipole moment sizes up a bond's polarity, and its arrow aims at the partially negative end.

questions.stem: State the polarity verdicts for CH3Cl and CCl4.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3Cl is polar, its dipoles summing toward chlorine; CCl4 is nonpolar, its four bond dipoles cancelling out.

questions.stem: Explain why bond polarity alone cannot decide molecular polarity.
questions.modelAnswer: Each bond dipole is a vector: identical dipoles arranged symmetrically sum to zero even though every bond is polar, so the molecules' geometry must enter the judgement alongside the bond polarities.

questions.stem: Predict whether CHCl3 (one H, three Cl on carbon) is polar, using the two-step method.
questions.modelAnswer: Step one: the three C-Cl bonds and one C-H bond are all polar. Step two: the asymmetric substitution leaves unbalanced dipoles with the resultant toward the chlorine side, so CHCl3 is polar.
